1st rowThe UC Davis ecosystem is fed by multiple upstream inputs: A. Academic Research Generated by UC Davis departments and institutes: CAES (College of Agricultural & Environmental Sciences) https://agriculture.ucdavis.edu/ Agricultural Sustainability Institute https://asi.ucdavis.edu/ These produce research in: soil science irrigation plant breeding climate resilience B. Public Research Funding Agricultural innovation systems rely heavily on public funding. Pardey et al. (2016) — Agricultural R&D https://www.nature.com/articles/537301a C. Real-World Agricultural Problems UC ANR connects directly to farmer needs across California: UC Cooperative Extension (county system) https://ucanr.edu/counties These local challenges (water, soil, yield, climate) drive research priorities. D. Applied Infrastructure Inputs Field-based systems provide real data: UC ANR Research & Extension Centers https://ucanr.edu/program/anr-research-and-extension-centers Russell Ranch Sustainable Agriculture Facility https://russellranch.ucdavis.edu/ Russell Ranch supports long-term farming systems research and field validation. E. Industry Demand California agriculture creates strong demand signals: California Agricultural Experiment Station https://aes.ucdavis.edu/ 🔷 UPSTREAM SUMMARY (FOR YOUR TABLE) UC Davis research Public funding (USDA, state) Farmer and industry needs Field infrastructure (testbeds, farms) Agricultural production systems

1st rowA. Farmers and Growers (PRIMARY) Knowledge is transferred through UC ANR: UC Cooperative Extension https://ucanr.edu/counties This is the main pathway from research → adoption (Extension Theory): Anderson & Feder (2004) https://academic.oup.com/wbro/article-abstract/19/1/41/1690292 B. Industry and Agribusiness Outputs flow into: Grower cooperatives food companies specialty crop systems California ag structure https://aes.ucdavis.edu/ C. Startups and Commercialization Through: UC Davis Venture Catalyst https://venturecatalyst.ucdavis.edu/ Innovation Institute for Food & Health https://foodandhealth.ucdavis.edu/ D. Policy and Public Systems Outputs inform: California Department of Food & Agriculture https://www.cdfa.ca.gov/ E. Talent Pipelines Graduate programs https://grad.ucdavis.edu/
2nd rowA. Farmers (Industrial Scale) Midwest row-crop producer Outputs: precision farming practices nutrient optimization strategies digital decision tools B. Agribusiness & Global Supply Chains ADM Corteva Bayer Outputs: seed technologies crop inputs processing systems C. Equipment & Precision Agriculture Systems John Deere Outputs: autonomous machinery sensor-driven systems precision application tools D. Financial & Commodity Systems (UNIQUE FEATURE) CME Group https://www.cmegroup.com/ Chicago Board of Trade https://www.cmegroup.com/company/cbot.html Outputs: commodity pricing risk management tools agricultural finance systems Role of commodity markets in agriculture https://www.cmegroup.com/education.html E. 1st row1. Research Creation UC Davis produces scientific knowledge https://agriculture.ucdavis.edu/ 2. Translation (Key Strength) UC ANR translates research into practical solutions https://ucanr.edu/ 3. Validation in Real Conditions Field testing happens through: Research & Extension Centers https://ucanr.edu/program/anr-research-and-extension-centers Russell Ranch https://russellranch.ucdavis.edu/ 4. Deployment Farmers and agribusiness adopt and scale solutions https://aes.ucdavis.edu/ 5. Innovation & Commercialization Startups and ventures emerge through: Venture Catalyst https://venturecatalyst.ucdavis.edu/ 6. Feedback Loop New challenges from farmers and industry feed back into research Agricultural Innovation Systems (World Bank) https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/cb73650c-7ef4-555c-af9b-6ca602b29266
2nd row1. Research Creation The system starts with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC), where knowledge is generated in: crop science soil systems agricultural engineering digital agriculture Key actors: College of ACES https://aces.illinois.edu Department of Crop Sciences https://cropsciences.illinois.edu/ Agricultural & Biological Engineering https://abe.illinois.edu/ These units generate both scientific and engineering knowledge, which is the foundation of the ecosystem. (UIUC research system): https://aces.illinois.edu/research/research 2. TRANSLATION (KEY DIFFERENTIATOR = DIGITAL LAYER) In Illinois, research is not translated mainly through extension (like UC Davis), but through data, AI, and engineering systems. Key actors: National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) https://www.ncsa.illinois.edu Center for Digital Agriculture https://digitalag.illinois.edu/ These convert research into: predictive models digital decision tools automation systems (digital agriculture transformation): https://digitalag.illinois.edu/about/ 3. DEPLOYMENT (REAL-WORLD APPLICATION) Technologies are deployed in large-scale Midwest farming systems (corn & soy). (U.S. production systems): https://www.ers.usda.gov/topics/crops/corn-and-other-feedgrains/ Farmers apply: precision agriculture variable rate inputs sensor-based systems Supporting deployment through extension: Illinois Extension https://extension.illinois.edu (extension role in adoption): https://academic.oup.com/wbro/article-abstract/19/1/41/1690292 4. INNOVATION & INDUSTRY SCALING Solutions are scaled and commercialized through: A. Corporates John Deere (machinery, automation) https://www.deere.com/ Corteva (seeds, inputs) https://www.corteva.com/ ADM (processing, value chains) https://www.adm.com/ B. Startup ecosystem Illinois Research Park https://researchpark.illinois.edu/ This enables: ag-tech startups digital agriculture companies C. Industry collaboration Center for Digital Agriculture works with industry + producers https://digitalag.illinois.edu/ (innovation systems): https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/entities/publication/cb73650c-7ef4-555c-af9b-6ca602b29266
